audits.mathematicalReason: The six equally likely labels give column-remainder counts (2,2,2) for columns (1,2,3), and row-remainder counts (2,2,1,1) for rows (1,2,3,4). Shading occurs when row and column have the same parity. The column is odd with probability 4/6, while the row is odd or even with probability 3/6 each. Independence therefore gives (4/6)(3/6) + (2/6)(3/6) = 1/2. Equivalently, 18 of the 36 equally likely ordered spin pairs succeed. Both listed routes are defensible alternatives; board cells themselves are not equally likely.

figureEvidence.fact: The wheel has six equal sectors labeled 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 9.
The board has columns 1–3 and rows 1–4; precisely the cells with matching row and column parity are shaded.

audits.mathematicalReason: Take the common tangent as horizontal. The original centers are 1 and 4 units above it and are 5 units apart, so their horizontal separation is √(5²−3²) = 4. For two externally tangent circles of radii u and v resting on this line, the horizontal separation of their centers is √((u+v)²−(u−v)²) = 2√(uv). The pictured third circle lies between the original centers' perpendicular projections, so its radius r satisfies 2√r + 4√r = 4. Thus r = 4/9. The diagram selects this gap configuration rather than a circle outside the two original circles.

figureEvidence.fact: All three circles lie above and touch the same horizontal tangent; the third circle occupies the small gap between the radius-1 and radius-4 circles and is externally tangent to both.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let L > 0 be the length of each straight side, w > 0 the rink width, and a the combined length of the two semicircular ends. Path R replaces each end arc of P by a two-chord chain, so R < P. Also P = 2L+a, whereas S = 2√(L²+w²)+a > P. Each of Q's two zigzag chains crosses the width twice. Reflecting the final segment across the side where it turns gives an endpoint displacement of 2w horizontally and L vertically, so each chain has length at least √(L²+4w²). Consequently Q ≥ 2√(L²+4w²)+a > S. This validates the listed shortest-segment, Pythagorean, and reflection method without assuming that Q's turning points are exact midpoints.

figureEvidence.fact: The four paths use congruent stadium-shaped rinks. P follows the boundary, while R retains the straight sides and replaces each semicircular end by two chords.
S uses both end semicircles and two full-length crossing diagonals. Q uses the same end semicircles and two top-to-bottom zigzag chains, each crossing the width twice.

audits.mathematicalReason: The large semicircle has area 2π, and the three smaller semicircles have total area 3π/2 before overlap correction. Adjacent small centers are one unit apart. Their upper intersection point therefore forms a unit equilateral triangle with the centers. Each upper overlap has area equal to two 60° unit sectors minus that triangle: π/3 − √3/4. There are two such positive-area overlaps; the outer small semicircles only touch, and there is no positive-area triple overlap. The shaded area is therefore 2π − 3π/2 + 2(π/3 − √3/4) = 7π/6 − √3/2. The sector-area assessment and supporting scopes fit this computation.

figureEvidence.fact: All four semicircles lie above AB. The three unit semicircles have centers at successive unit positions along the length-4 diameter, and the shading is outside their union.
Only neighboring small semicircles overlap in positive area; the leftmost and rightmost meet at the midpoint of AB.

audits.mathematicalReason: Use the complete 6-by-6 repeating block at the displayed corner. It contains 12 fully dark unit squares and 8 dark half-squares, giving dark area 12 + 8/2 = 16 out of total area 36. Thus the dark fraction is 16/36 = 4/9. The identical-corner condition supplies matching period boundaries, so this fraction applies to the whole floor, not merely to an arbitrary cropped sample. Combining the component areas and interpreting the resulting fraction are both directly represented by the proposed assessed scopes.

figureEvidence.fact: The upper-left 6-by-6 grid block repeats horizontally and vertically. Its dark areas by successive rows are 1, 2, 5, 5, 2, and 1 unit-square areas.
Within that block, the partial dark cells are eight triangular halves of unit squares, in addition to twelve completely dark squares.

audits.mathematicalReason: Since 5²+12²=13², angle C is right and triangle ABC has area 30. Also AM=1 and BN=8. The right corner triangles AMJ and BNK are similar to ABC, with hypotenuse scale factors 1/13 and 8/13 respectively. Hence the pentagon's area is 30[1−(1/13)²−(8/13)²] = 240/13. The coordinate alternative is also valid: with C=(0,0), A=(0,5), and B=(12,0), line AB is 5x+12y=60. The perpendicular feet are J=(60/169,820/169) and K=(876/169,480/169), which give the same area by shoelace. These are alternative routes, not a required union of methods.

figureEvidence.fact: M and N are on AC and BC, and the right-angle marks place J and K as their perpendicular feet on AB.
The boundary order is C–M–J–K–N; the pentagon is triangle ABC with corner triangles AMJ and BNK removed.

audits.mathematicalReason: Each section side is a face segment with perpendicular components 1 and 1/2, so all four sides have length √5/2 and ABCD is a rhombus. Its diagonals are the cube's body diagonal AC=√3 and the horizontal diagonal BD=√2. Its area is therefore AC·BD/2 = √6/2. Alternatively, splitting along BD produces two isosceles triangles, each with base √2 and height √((√5/2)²−(√2/2)²)=√3/2. Adding their areas gives the same result and directly supports the composite-area assessment. Both proposed routes are valid.

figureEvidence.fact: A is the lower front-left vertex and C the upper back-right vertex. B and D lie halfway up the back-left and front-right vertical edges, respectively.
Successive section sides lie on the four vertical cube faces, while B and D are at the same height on horizontally opposite edges.

audits.mathematicalReason: Fold the original three-square row into three successive side faces; its square below the left end occupies a fourth face. Attachments at positions 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9 each place the added square on a previously unused face, giving valid five-face cube nets. Position 1 folds onto the face already occupied by the rightmost original square, and position 3 folds onto the face occupied by the original lower square. Position 2 creates a 2-by-2 block, which cannot fold into four distinct cube faces. Thus exactly six positions work. Testing partial cube nets is directly within the proposed scope.

figureEvidence.fact: The four original shaded squares consist of a horizontal row of three and one square immediately below the row's leftmost square.

Positions 1, 2, and 3 are respectively below the original lower square, below the row's middle square, and below the row's rightmost square. Positions 4–9 are the other labeled boundary attachments shown.
